newsitem.title: USA: No quick cure seen for Thailand's "hot money" woes.
newsitem.headline: No quick cure seen for Thailand's "hot money" woes.

text.p: A flush of flighty short-term capital, testing the mettle of Thailand's economic and monetary authorities is likely to remain a source of instability, U.S. market experts say.

Moody's Investors Service Inc downgraded Thailand's short-term currency debt rating to Prime-2 from Prime-1 on Tuesday, citing "the very rapid and recent accumulation of short-term external debt" that has made the country vulnerable to a financial shock.
While Thailand must address the current account deficits and inflation problems to restore its credit standing, the intractable free flows of hot money defy easy solutions, the experts said.
Foreign investors stepped up purchases of short-term baht instruments since Thailand liberalized its financial markets in 1993, said Hanan Salem, sovereign analyst at Moody's.
"It is a price to pay for opening up the financial sector to foreign investment," she said, noting that Korea and Chile ran into smiliar problems.

The excess liquidity and inflation boost interest rates. Speculators could pick up 400 basis points in yields over U.S. Treasuries without running much of a currency risk, because of Thailand's policy of basing its exchange rate on a basket of major currencies.
The Thai authorities have not had much success with attempts to solve these problems through administrative measures such as putting presssure on banks to borrow longer-term, Salem said.

While hot money pours into Thailand from all quarters, Japanese banks and domestic Thai corporations have made the most of the arbitrage yield play, said Luis R. Luis, director of emerging market research as Scudder Stevenson Clark.
The central bank of Thailand has limited options to tinker with the currency, because an appreciation would worsen the already huge current account deficit, he said.
Moody's downgrade was a prudent warning to all investors, Luis said.
Feroz Talyarkhan, Asian fixed income analyst at Bear, Stearns and Co Inc, noted that Thailand's short-term debt rating at Prime-2 is still very solid, far from approaching the danger zone.
Moody's rating scale on short-term debt runs from Prime-1, Prime-2, and Prime-3 to "not prime". Thailand's Prime-2 rating puts it in a league with China, Chile, Israel and Kuwait.
With $39 billion in reserves, the central bank has weathered two large-scale attacks, with one in January 1995 and the other in July this year, Talyarkhan said.
In addition, Southeast Asian central banks have formed a mutual support group to lend to each other in times of need, he said.
"A sustained run cannot develop," he said, adding that foreign banks were the ones that got bloodied in each attack.
Still, currency traders expected recurrent bouts of volatility as long as Thai interest rates stay high and the baht relatively stable.
The alliance of central banks remains an untested "gentlemen's agreement," said an Asian currency trader at a U.S. money center bank.

"There's so much speculative capital around, and you get 'Soros Wannabes,'" he said, referring to the legendary hedge fund speculator George Soros, who successfully bet on sterling's devaluation in 1992.
